transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-14 15:00 UTC; Duration: ~57m; Recording: yes
Attendees: Alice Coleman (Redwood AE), Ravi Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Arcadia ML), Diego Rivera (Arcadia Infra), Noah Bennett (Arcadia CTO)

Summary:
Quick-engineering deep dive focused on conversational state stitching (how session context is assembled from KV), unusual long-tail eviction patterns Arcadia is seeing, and options for graceful fallback to disk/on-prem store without violating latency SLOs. Discussed routed batching tradeoffs, prefetch hints, and the impact of different quantization profiles on resident KV size.

Topics captured: KV layout, prefix cardinality, eviction watermarking, async prefetch, SSD spillback protocol, sticky routing, telemetry needed for root-cause.

Transcript body:
00:00 Alice Coleman: Hey everyone thanks for joining. We thought it'd be helpful to run through the session stitching problem you described and map it to the KV layout in the Redwood runtime. Rough agenda: sketch-arch, telemetry you have, then remedies.
00:18 Maya Chen: yeah appreciate it, our users are hitting avging latency spikes — a small percent of requests go from 90ms to 1.2s and it basically lines up with cache misses on large conversations.
00:30 Ravi Shah: okay so when you say "large conversations" do you mean long token sequences or lots of prefix reuse across many users?
00:36 Maya Chen: mostly long token sequences — like 6 to 12k tokens over multi-turn sessions — but we also have a lot of shared system prompts and templates that create hot prefixes.
00:47 Diego Rivera: and from infra side we've seen the tokenstore resident set grow and then suddenly a spike of eviction churn which we think correlates to a spilling operation that locks the slab for a bit.
00:58 Noah Bennett: putting that in context, we run in a private VPC with on-prem HSM for keys; anything that causes extra egress to disk is a risk for us. Latency SLOs are strict.
01:12 Alice Coleman: right got it. Quick sketch: the Redwood runtime keeps a KV store keyed by conversation-prefix fingerprint — a compact token hash — with LRU-ish eviction plus a watermark-based spill. But depending on prefix cardinality and the shard placement, you can get hot-spot eviction.
01:30 Maya Chen: "LRU-ish" is the phrase I saw in the docs, that's part of the surprise — it looks non-deterministic in our traces.
01:38 Ravi Shah: yeah the runtime uses a multi-tier retention policy: small in-memory slab per shard, per-prefix TTL heuristics, and a global backpressure watermark. The heuristics attempt to keep long-context KV entries sticky if they are accessed in the last X minutes. But that X is adaptive and might be too aggressive under sustained bursts.
01:58 Diego Rivera: we observed prefix reuse across unrelated sessions — the same system prompt hash appears across many user sessions and that is making that prefix artificially hot leading to eviction of other unique long-context entries.
02:10 Noah Bennett: so is that a namespace collision or expected? We thought prefix was scoped by tenant.
02:17 Ravi Shah: by default it's per-tenant but if you use shared templates (Arcadia does), the runtime stores the canonical prompt once and references it which reduces memory, but it does increase the apparent popularity (and thus hotness) of that prefix in the shard it lands on.
02:33 Maya Chen: ah okay that explains the hot spot. So we have a mix: a few extremely common prefixes and a long tail of large unique ctxs that should remain resident but instead get evicted.
02:45 Alice Coleman: two angles to consider: 1) change routing so hot prefixes are replicated or pinned across shards to avoid eviction pressure (pin small hot entries), or 2) change eviction policy to prefer evicting shared small prefixes less aggressively while guessing which large entries are cold. Both have tradeoffs.
03:02 Diego Rivera: replicating sounds expensive for us, memory is at a premium on our Dedicated nodes. Also pinned replication intersects with our VPC isolation constraints.
03:12 Ravi Shah: understood. Another option is adaptive prefetch hints: your inference layer can send a prefetch hint for the next N_kv prefixes when a conversation enters an "active long-context" state. That lets the runtime prefetch asynchronously from SSD or remote KV and warm the slab ahead of demand.
03:30 Maya Chen: will prefetch help if the slab is thrashing? If we prefetch too aggressively won't we cause more eviction?
03:38 Ravi Shah: good point. The runtime supports prefetch with a low-priority tenant where prefetched entries are tagged 'soft' and are the first to be evicted. The heuristic: prefetched soft entries give you fast hits if the conversation continues but won't displace 'hard' resident long-context tokens. That requires the prefetch to use a different retention bucket.
03:58 Noah Bennett: okay I want to make sure we don't end up with the prefetch causing more churn. Can we throttle prefetch concurrency per-tenant?
04:06 Ravi Shah: yes per-tenant prefetch concurrency and a global circuit-breaker exist. You can set prefetch concurrency to 1–2 tasks per shard. Also there's an adaptive backoff when eviction rate exceeds threshold.
04:20 Maya Chen: what's the impact to latency for async prefetch misses? If a request hits and the KV isn't resident, does the runtime block on a fetch from remote disk?
04:27 Ravi Shah: there's a non-blocking fast path: if a critical prefix isn't present, the runtime will try local slab fetch, if miss it will trigger an async prefetch and either 1) fall back to compacted context reconstruction (re-encode from checkpointed deltas) or 2) stall for up to a small configurable bound to wait for hot fetch. We typically set that stall bound to keep p99 under SLO — say 200ms.
04:53 Diego Rivera: that stall is the scary bit — some of our spikes look like those stalls. They're in the 600–1200ms range though.
05:02 Ravi Shah: those larger stalls usually mean remote fetch is hitting cold SSD or contention on the slab due to lock-induced delays. We had a case where the slab eviction did a snapshot to persistent store with a pause.
05:14 Maya Chen: snapshot to persistent store? I thought eviction is just dropping keys.
05:18 Ravi Shah: usually yes, but in on-prem deployments with persistence enabled, the runtime performs an append-of-deleted to the on-disk store for recovery; under certain compaction windows that can cause brief I/O spikes. We can tune compaction schedule or disable immediate write-on-evict.
05:34 Noah Bennett: that sounds like a configuration we need to control carefully in our VPC. Any recommended defaults for on-prem?
05:40 Ravi Shah: for on-prem we recommend asynchronous background compaction at low IO priority and a jittered schedule to avoid synchronized compaction across nodes. Also separate the persistent store to a different physical device than the model weights to avoid head-of-line blocking.
05:56 Alice Coleman: another lever: quantization. If you can move to narrower quant (e.g., int8->int4 for KV payloads when safe), you can shrink resident size and reduce eviction. But quantization can increase CPU decode time a little, a cost-latency tradeoff.
06:13 Maya Chen: we use 8-bit for model weights, but our KV payload also includes compressed token embeddings when we store deltas — can we quantize those?
06:21 Ravi Shah: yes but be careful — embedding quantization to 4-bit works for many use-cases but introduces small fidelity loss which can affect reranking. We recommend running a quality block test on your eval set; Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles by workload.
06:38 Diego Rivera: pricing-wise, replicating pinned prefixes isn't attractive. Are there cheaper options?
06:44 Alice Coleman: yes the cheaper options are smarter eviction policies (age-based with access-frequency), tiered-slabs (small hot slab + large long-term slab backed by slower SSD), and prefix shadowing — keep a small bloom filter or pointer in memory for very large prefixes and fetch full payload on-demand.
07:03 Maya Chen: explain prefix shadowing — sounds promising.
07:07 Ravi Shah: prefix shadowing stores a compact pointer and a micro-signature in fast memory; actual payload is on SSD. When a request references the prefix we check the micro-signature then asynchronously load the payload. If it becomes hot, it gets promoted to the fast slab. Shadowing avoids reserving full memory for rarely-used big contexts.
07:23 Diego Rivera: what's the cost of micro-signature checks CPU-wise? We're already CPU constrained on the inference hosts.
07:30 Ravi Shah: negligible compared to token generation. It's a small hash check per request, inlined and vectorized. The overhead is in the IO when a promotion happens, not the micro-check itself.
07:41 Maya Chen: sounds like a combination of shadowing + soft-prefetching might solve our tail without replication.
07:47 Alice Coleman: agreed, and add per-prefix prioritization: system prompts get 'keep' flags so they're less likely to be evicted; long unique contexts get sticky tags if accessed N times in M minutes.
07:59 Noah Bennett: what about routed batching? We've noticed that at high QPS, batching can amplify the effect of eviction because many requests reference the same shard at once and generate a burst of KV requests.
08:12 Ravi Shah: routed batching groups requests for model invocation but also attempts to coalesce KV fetches. The runtime has a coalescer that dedupes simultaneous fetches for the same prefix. But if the requests target many unique prefixes, batching increases concurrency and thus pressure on slab. There are knobs: max-batch-window, coalesce-window, and a batch-prefetch threshold.
08:34 Diego Rivera: if we reduce batch window to lower memory spikes, won't throughput fall?
08:38 Ravi Shah: yes there's a tradeoff: smaller batch windows lower latency and spike memory usage but can reduce throughput efficiency. We normally recommend dynamic batch windows that widen under steady traffic and shrink on bursty patterns.
08:49 Maya Chen: how can we detect bursty patterns effectively? We have some telemetry but not sure which metric to track for dynamic windows.
08:55 Ravi Shah: track prefix-uniq-per-second per-shard and slab-evictions-per-minute. If uniq-prefix/sec spikes above a threshold relative to slab size, shrink batch window and increase soft-prefetch budget.
09:10 Alice Coleman: quick pause — can we look at the telemetry files you shared earlier?
09:15 Diego Rivera: sure I uploaded a small sample to the shared drive, link in the chat. The file has per-shard eviction counters, average slab occupancy, and miss latency.
09:28 Ravi Shah: scanning... I can already see a correlation: around 2026-01-08 02:00 UTC, slab occupancy hits 92% and eviction rate climbs; at the same time miss-latency jumps. The eviction is not uniform — it's heavy on shards 3 and 7 which suggests skewed hashing.
09:46 Maya Chen: we use a simple modulo mapping on session-id right now which can produce skew.
09:52 Ravi Shah: switching to rendezvous hashing or adding a consistent-hash salt per-tenant can reduce shard-hotspots. Also consider a hot-prefix cache that bypasses the normal shard mapping for the most-frequently-used N prefixes.
10:06 Diego Rivera: would a hot-prefix bypass break our VPC pinning semantics? We rely on topology to keep tenant data within a fixed node pool.
10:14 Ravi Shah: it can — you'd need to ensure hot-prefix replicas are only placed on nodes within the same VPC/tenant pool. The runtime can be configured for tenant-local replication.
10:26 Alice Coleman: on the telemetry side, Ravi will provide an export with per-prefix frequencies and a bloom of top-1k prefixes to help you identify candidates for pinning.
10:36 Ravi Shah: noted. A few more lower-level points: 1) reduce synchronous writes on evict, 2) enable slab partitioning to avoid global lock during eviction, 3) set eviction watermark as percent of shard-reserved memory rather than global.
10:51 Maya Chen: what about TTL heuristics — ours seem to drop entries too early even if recently used within the same converstation but outside the last X minutes.
10:58 Ravi Shah: the heuristics use an access score combining recency and frequency with a session-affinity multiplier if the same session touches it repeatedly. We can tune the session-affinity window to your session lengths. For example bumping affinity from 5m to 20m would keep those long conversations resident longer.
11:17 Diego Rivera: any gotchas when tuning affinity windows?
11:21 Ravi Shah: larger affinity windows mean less churn but more memory consumption — you'll trade off overall hit-rate distribution. Also, if many sessions are long, increasing affinity across the board can blow the resident set. Better to target affinity bump only when prefix size exceeds a threshold (i.e., large payloads get longer affinity).
11:38 Noah Bennett: earlier you mentioned a handoff protocol for spillback to SSD. Can you sketch that?
11:44 Ravi Shah: yes: conceptually, on eviction we don't eagerly delete; instead we write a tombstone + pointer to SSD snapshot. The pointer includes a generation id and optional eviction signature. On access, we attempt a non-blocking restore: check pointer, if SSD object present schedule async load, in meantime return compacted context. If load completes within the stall bound promote to slab. If not, keep compacted fallback. The key is making SSD restores idempotent and rate-limited so they don't amplify spikes.
12:14 Maya Chen: that seems safe. We just need to ensure the SSD path is within our VPC and doesn't breach compliance.
12:20 Alice Coleman: Redwood Private supports placement of persistent store within the customer VPC; we can provide the architecture note. I'll attach it.
12:28 Diego Rivera: final question — any quick wins we can toggle today?
12:31 Ravi Shah: yes: 1) enable soft-prefetch with low concurrency, 2) increase session-affinity window for large payloads, 3) switch to consistent hashing salt, 4) disable synchronous write-on-evict. Those are low-risk and reversible.
12:46 Maya Chen: great. Let's try those and run the 24h soak. We'll also produce flamegraphs.
12:51 Alice Coleman: perfect. Recap of next steps: Redwood exports telemetry and example configs; Arcadia runs soak and shares traces; follow-up scheduled for two weeks to review results.
12:59 Noah Bennett: thanks all — appreciate the practical knobs.
13:04 Alice Coleman: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and the telemetry export. Bye.

End of transcript.
